newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Election commission snubs court in Serbia crisis.
newsitem.headline: Election commission snubs court in Serbia crisis.

text.p: Thousands of people marched on Wednesday in renewed protests against election rigging in Serbia as the electoral commission in one town, snubbing a court order, reversed an opposition victory.
The court ruling had initially been read as a sign that President Slobodan Milosevic was starting to bow to pressure from a month of street protests against alleged election fraud.
But the electoral commission in Smederevska Palanka confirmed the ruling socialists as winners of local elections in November, an independent Belgrade radio station reported.

"The town election commission completely ignored the court order...and confirmed the Socialists' victory," Dragan Blagojevic, a leader of the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition and a member of the commission, told radio B92.
"I told them 20 times they cannot vote on the court order, that they have to respect the law. They just smiled," he said.
The district court ruled on Monday that Zajedno should be awarded victory in the election in the southeastern town and it ordered the socialist-dominated commission to comply.
Zajedno says it won 15 of Serbia's biggest towns and cities, including Belgrade, in the November 17 local elections, only to have the triumphs reversed by socialist manipulation.
Milosevic pledged on Tuesday to investigate Zajedno's claims of vote rigging in a move interpreted as an indication that he was giving way to popular protests and Western displeasure.
The Smederevska Palanka decision was bound to infuriate tens of thousands of Zajedno supporters who demonstrated across Serbia on Wednesday for a 31st successive day.
In Belgrade, some 30,000 students marched on Dedinje, the exclusive residential area that houses Milosevic and members of his ruling elite, for the second time in a week.
Police in riot gear politely but resolutely turned them back as they approached the district, continuing the measured policy that has characterised their behaviour since the protests began.
"Today we are checking if citizens of Belgrade can freely walk in their town or if there are zones to which ordinary mortals are forbidden access," one of the students told police.
In anticipation of being blocked in their march, the students carried a large cardboard pyramid inscribed: "Forbidden City, No Trespassing."
More than 100,000 Zajedno supporters later took to the streets, jeering as they paraded past the Russian embassy because of Moscow's support of Milosevic.
The daily demonstrations drew up to 250,000 people in Belgrade last weekend and have spread to more than 30 towns and cities.
Washington has led Western attacks on Milosevic's effective one-party rule in Serbia, demanding that he should accept defeat in Belgrade and other cities.

Popular pressure and Western displeasure seemed to be behind Milosevic's pledge to students, who trekked on foot for 230 km (145 miles) to meet him, that he would investigate opposition protests about vote rigging.

"Neither you nor I count votes, but I shall ask the government to instruct the justice ministry to study very carefully all the facts contained in the documents which you have given me," he told the students to Tuesday.

In the southern town of Vranje, traditionally a socialist bastion, party activists managed to round up only a few hundred people for a rally in support of Milosevic. "There were more flags and slogans than people," one Zajedno supporter said.
